title: We're getting married and planning kids. How do we keep building our property portfolio?
excerpt: An engaged couple with three properties between them want three each. Sean says use the one 90% loan slot left, then pause and budget for the wedding, the birth and childcare.

question.asker: From Mr K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr K, 32, earns RM6,000 a month and has bought a RM500,000 home near PJ for his own use, due in early 2026, with a RM2,000 instalment. He also owns a unit worth about RM150,000, rented at RM700 against a RM300 instalment. His fiancée, 31, earns RM9,000 and has a RM380,000 unit due in mid 2025 that she plans to rent out. They have saved about RM150,000, plan a small wedding this year and hope for one or two children.
question.text: What would Sean do in their shoes, starting a family while wanting three properties each?

answer.quote: Focus on your wife's second 90% slot first, then call it a day.
answer.summary: They are already well placed with three properties. Use her remaining 90% loan slot, consider selling the RM150,000 unit that ties up one of his, and then pause buying for three to five years while they budget for the wedding, the birth and childcare and invest in their health, knowledge and insurance.

reasons.title: Three properties, one every decade
reasons.body: Sean's goal for every Malaysian is three properties by retirement: one to live in, one to sell for living costs and one for emergencies or a child's education. Buying one around 30, 40 and 50 is enough, and the first is usually paid off by 60.

reasons.title: A cheap unit wastes a 90% slot
reasons.body: Each person gets only two loans at a 90% margin. Holding a RM150,000 unit on one of them blocks a larger purchase his income could support, though there's no rush to sell.

reasons.title: A baby costs more than you expect
reasons.body: Sean's son's delivery in a private hospital cost about RM15,000 to RM18,000, confinement centres charge about RM13,000 to RM15,000 a month and premium ones RM20,000 or more, and daycare costs him about RM1,800 a month.

reasons.title: Small monthly savings rebuild a down payment
reasons.body: Putting aside RM1,000 a month builds RM48,000 in four years, enough for a down payment. Their portfolio can run on its own while the children are young, and they can buy again once they are at school.

actions: Budget RM30,000 to RM40,000 for her unit's handover fees and renovation, and check whether the MOT is included in the sales package.
Agree a wedding budget early; Sean suggests a simple wedding and more travel before the baby arrives.
Budget for the birth, confinement and childcare at the higher end first; cheaper options are a choice you can make later.
Use her second 90% loan slot carefully, then pause buying for three to five years.
Save a fixed sum each month, and invest in your health, your knowledge and enough insurance for both breadwinners.
caveat: These are Sean's own family's costs and choices, and parents or in-laws who can help with childcare cut the budget a lot. Whether the RM150,000 unit should go depends on what they would buy with the freed slot.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #238. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in January 2024, and the baby costs are Sean's own experience. Sean works with The Makeover Guys, the renovation company the viewer mentions.
